headings.title: Introduction to Geriatric Homes and Residential Care
headings.content: Geriatric homes provide residential and specialized care for older adults who can no longer live independently. These facilities bridge the gap between hospital care and independent living, offering structured support with daily activities. As Nigeria experiences a growing aging population due to rising life expectancy, traditional family care systems face increasing economic and logistical strain. Consequently, formal residential care is slowly gaining acceptance as a viable alternative for older adults requiring continuous supervision. Facilities range from basic assisted living setups to skilled nursing homes equipped to handle complex medical needs. Understanding this landscape helps nurses advocate for appropriate placement and optimal resource utilization for elderly clients.

headings.title: The Role of the Home Healthcare Nurse in Geriatric Facilities
headings.content: Nurses in geriatric facilities function as caregivers, care coordinators, educators, and patient advocates. Daily responsibilities include monitoring vital signs, administering medications, coordinating multidisciplinary care plans, and supervising care assistants. A key nursing duty involves observing subtle behavioral or physical changes that signal early infection or cognitive decline. Nurses also act as a vital communication link between residents, families, and attending physicians.

headings.title: Comprehensive Health Assessment of the Older Adult
headings.content:
Assessing an older adult requires a holistic approach known as a Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA). This evaluation covers physical health, functional capacity, psychological status, and social circumstances. 

- **Functional Status**: Assesses **Activities of Daily Living (ADLs)** such as bathing, feeding, and dressing, alongside **Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs)** like managing finances and cooking.
- **Mental Health**: Screens for common issues like depression, delirium, and dementia using validated screening tools.
- **Environmental Assessment**: Evaluates living spaces for hazards that compromise safety.

headings.title: Promoting Mobility and Preventing Falls in Geriatric Homes
headings.content:
Falls are a leading cause of morbidity, loss of independence, and mortality among older adults. Physiological changes like decreased muscle mass (**sarcopenia**), poor balance, and visual impairments elevate fall risks. Medications such as sedatives and antihypertensives further contribute to postural hypotension and dizziness.

| Intervention Type | Examples |
|---|---| 
| Environmental | Clearing pathways, ensuring bright lighting, installing grab bars | 
| Clinical | Medication reviews, regular vision and hearing checks | 
| Physical | Structured balance exercises, assistive device provision |

headings.title: Managing Chronic Conditions and Polypharmacy
headings.content: Most residents in geriatric homes manage multiple chronic illnesses such as hypertension, diabetes, osteoarthritis, and heart failure. Treating these conditions often leads to **polypharmacy**, the concurrent use of multiple medications by a patient. Polypharmacy significantly increases the likelihood of adverse drug reactions, drug-drug interactions, and medication non-adherence due to complex dosing schedules. Nurses play a crucial role in medication reconciliation, monitoring for toxicity, and communicating with prescribers to simplify regimens whenever possible.

headings.title: Nutrition, Hydration, and Dietary Management for Residents
headings.content: Nutritional status directly impacts wound healing, immune function, and overall strength in older adults. Age-related factors like reduced taste sensitivity, dental loss, swallowing difficulties (**dysphagia**), and decreased gastrointestinal motility often lead to malnutrition and dehydration. Facilities must offer modified food textures and nutrient-dense meals. Nurses should monitor daily fluid intake, assist residents who cannot feed themselves, and watch for unintended weight loss.

headings.title: Palliative Care and End-of-Life Considerations
headings.content: Palliative care in geriatric homes focuses on improving the quality of life for residents facing life-limiting illnesses. Rather than curative efforts, the goal shifts to comfort, pain management, symptom control, and psychological and spiritual support. Nurses facilitate advanced care planning, respect resident autonomy, and provide compassionate support to grieving families. Ensuring a dignified, pain-free death is a core tenet of professional geriatric nursing practice.

headings.title: Ethical, Legal, and Quality Improvement Standards in Nigeria
headings.content: Geriatric facilities operate under ethical and legal frameworks that protect resident rights, dignity, and safety. Nurses must uphold confidentiality, obtain informed consent, and prevent elder abuse or neglect. Regulatory bodies in Nigeria, such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) and state health ministries, set standards for operational compliance. Regular quality improvement audits ensure that hygiene, staffing ratios, and clinical protocols meet acceptable healthcare benchmarks.
